title: Christ the King
hookLine: the last Sunday of the church year: a king crowned with thorns

lines: A SOLDIER TWISTS A RING OF THORNS.
A CORONATION, STAGED AS A JOKE.
THE LAST SUNDAY OF THE CHURCH YEAR.
cards: A soldier is twisting thorn branches into a ring, carefully, so it holds its shape. Around him, the rest of the band are laughing. They have found a scarlet robe.
Someone has a reed for a scepter. The prisoner is already beaten and tired, and they are about to crown him. A whole coronation, staged as a joke, in a governor's hall in Jerusalem.
On the last Sunday of the church year, before Advent starts the circle again, Catholic and some Protestant churches keep a feast for the man under those thorns: Christ the King.

teach.b: Look at what the soldiers do.

Matthew tells it, in the King James words: "And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!"
Crown, scepter, robe, a bended knee, a royal greeting: every part of a real coronation, all meant as mockery. Christians say the joke was true, and the soldiers didn't know it.
Then the sign. John says Pilate wrote a title and had it put on the cross: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Meant as a charge; read by Christians as a proclamation.
Earlier that same morning, Pilate had asked Jesus straight out whether he was a king.

teach.h: MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.
teach.b: Jesus answered: "My kingdom is not of this world." Not that it isn't real, Christians say, but that it doesn't come from here, and doesn't run on the same rules. Its king doesn't send soldiers.
He washes feet. In Mark, Jesus says he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life. So this feast turns a crown upside down.

Paul, writing to the church at Philippi, says Jesus took the form of a servant, went all the way down to death on a cross, and that God lifted him high, so "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow."
The soldiers bowed the knee to mock him. Paul says every knee should bow, this time in earnest. Same motion, opposite meaning.

how: Catholic and some Protestant churches keep Christ the King on the last Sunday before Advent, with readings about Christ's kingship and hymns that call him king, and some end the service with a procession.

o: an attendant who waits on a king at court
a king who wins his throne by conquering foes
a king who rules by serving, crowned with thorns

games.q: the soldiers' coronation — tap the pairs.
p: a reed in his right hand
my kingdom is not of this world

s: the soldiers put the crown of thorns on Jesus as an honor
they mocked him: hail, King of the Jews.
in Matthew, the soldiers bow the knee before Jesus
they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him.
Jesus tells Pilate his kingdom is of this world
he says the opposite: my kingdom is not of this world.

games.q: Pilate asks Jesus straight out whether he is a king. what does Jesus answer?
o: no. I am only a teacher.
my kingdom is not of this world.
games.why: in John's Gospel he answers, my kingdom is not of this world. not unreal, Christians say, but not from here, and not run on the same rules.

practice: Picture the ring of thorns and the reed, then someone in your own life who served without a crown: a nurse on a night shift, a parent at a sink, a neighbor who shoveled your path. Slowly lower your head.
If you pray, bow to Christ the King with Paul's words, at the name of Jesus every knee should bow; if you don't, let the bow be thanks for everyone who serves.

wordCard.voice: Servant king. The feast's name for a king crowned with thorns, who came not to be served but to serve, and whose kingdom is not of this world.

orig.note: Greek: king. the word on the sign over the cross in John's Gospel: the King of the Jews.

carryVoice: Your line: a different king. His crown was made of thorns. Rest well.
